extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics graduate students, and authors preparing mathematical papers, books, or theses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for clear, precise, and professional mathematical writing: sentence-level style, logical phrasing, grammar/usage rules, and presentation of formulas for papers, books, and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'then' as logical connective and signpost
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'then' is pivotal to the logical structure; it acts both as a connective and as a sign post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit 'then' expecting the reader to supply it. Make implications explicit so the reader need not infer logical flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place hypotheses inside the proposition to be proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrasing exercises like 'If f is a continuous function, then prove X' when what is intended is 'Prove that, if f is a continuous function, then X.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it clear whether the hypothesis is part of the assumptions of the exercise or part of the conclusion to be demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining terms: typographic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When you define a term (for the first time), italicize the word or phrase that is being defined; when you refer to a word as an object of discussion, put it in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Use italics for a new definition; quote words like 'the' when discussing the word itself. Follow these conventions for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of 'if and only if'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If and only if' indicates logical equivalence and should be treated with deference; avoid beginning a sentence with this phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer placing 'if and only if' within the sentence (e.g., 'A real number x has a real square root if and only if x ≥ 0'), or use alternate phrasings ('Nonnegative real numbers, and only those, have real square roots'). The abbreviation 'iff' or the symbol ⇐⇒ are acceptable in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word order matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Word order can alter meaning or nuance; different word orders emphasize different aspects of a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proofreading, read aloud and check whether word order conveys the intended emphasis and meaning; watch how inserting small words (like 'only') changes meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud to catch obscurities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors tend to supply missing meaning when reading their own work; reading aloud helps reveal obscurities imposed by word order or structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aloud reading as a proofreading technique to expose sentences that rely on reader-supplied inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overusing commas; use them for logical pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not insert commas merely to mark breath pauses; commas should indicate logical pauses, not lack of air or poor sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences with spurious commas into clearer, shorter sentences or properly structured clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary 'given'; prefer explicit conditional phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians overuse 'given' in ways that transcribe spoken laziness into writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct conditional sentences like 'If X is a metric space and p∈X, then ...' rather than 'Given a metric space X, and a point p in X, ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer singular constructions for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, use singular rather than plural constructions to avoid ambiguity about whether collectivities share properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., replace 'Domains with noncompact automorphism groups have orbit accumulation points in their boundaries' with 'A domain with noncompact automorphism group has an orbit accumulation point in its boundary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance prose and calculations; interleave for ease of reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Several consecutive pages of dense prose or tedious calculation are not appealing; interweave prose and formulas to give comfortable stopping places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide frequent breathers (short paragraphs, displayed formulas, commentary) so readers can pause and reflect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use displayed math for long or important formulas; number if referenced later
rubrics_metrics.description: Long formulas are usually better displayed; important formulas should be displayed regardless of length and labeled if they will be mentioned later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not display every formula (this makes the paper cumbersome) and do not inline every formula (this makes writing tedious). Strike a balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider language habits of non-native readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because English is the language of choice in mathematics, native speakers should exercise care so that non-native readers are not misled by informal spoken idioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid colloquialisms like 'cook up a function'; prefer conventional phrasing that non-native speakers can readily interpret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pretension: prefer simple words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid big or obscure words when small ones will do; do not use long words merely to display erudition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful many readers are non-native speakers; write simple, straightforward English that will be easily apprehended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to simple sentence structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex sentence structures (even subjunctive mood) can lead to confusion in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, declarative, short sentences and short paragraphs, each making a single point; break up dense arguments into palatable bites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flippancy and sarcasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarcastic or flippant remarks in mathematical writing (insults, coarse humor) are unwise and may embarrass the author later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tone professional: reviewers, advisors, and later readers will view such language unfavorably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit tone to the subject; avoid faddish or dated expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose vocabulary and tone appropriate to the subject; avoid slang, political fads, or archaic expressions that will date or confuse your writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign phrases should be used sparingly and typeset in italics; avoid expressions that will be meaningless to future readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of person: default to 'we' (first person plural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern mathematical custom is to use the first person plural 'we' to stress participation and to be less jarring than 'I' or 'one'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'I' rarely (e.g., to state personal knowledge), avoid awkward 'one' constructions, and consider rephrasing to eliminate pronouns altogether when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and usage are tools, not the primary goal
rubrics_metrics.description: While exact use of language is important, the main goal is logical and cogent writing; grammar rules are tools that aid clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and apply rules judiciously; override them when strict correctness produces awkward phrasing, but use good sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier precision: avoid 'any' when 'all/each/every' is meant
rubrics_metrics.description: Misuse of quantifiers can cause serious misunderstanding (e.g., 'any' may be read as 'some').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'each', 'every', or 'all' when universal quantification is intended, and check statements for unintended readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity: prefer concise phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate thoughts briefly and succinctly; eliminate extraneous wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what each word adds; if a sentence says the same in fewer words, prefer the shorter; consult Strunk & White for principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Latin abbreviations (cf., e.g., i.e., n.b., q.v.) with care
rubrics_metrics.description: These abbreviations have specific meanings and punctuation/font implications; they are often misused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer English equivalents if unsure; be accurate with 'cf.' (compare) versus 'see', and 'e.g.' (for example) vs 'i.e.' (that is).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprise vs compose: use 'comprise' correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct usage: 'A comprises B' (A comprises its parts). Avoid 'is comprised of'; use 'is composed of' instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., correct: 'The standing committee comprises two women, three men, and a donkey.' Incorrect: 'The committee is comprised of ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contractions in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractions like 'don't', 'can't' are taboo in formal writing; avoid informal abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractions may be acceptable in informal writing to create a friendly tone, but formal mathematical writing should avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'denote' only for specific representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'denote' when a specific symbol stands for a specific item; do not use 'denote' as a synonym for 'let' or 'be'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'Let X denote the set of ...' is acceptable when X specifically represents that set; avoid 'Denote X the set of all left-handed polyglots.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misusing unfamiliar words (e.g., 'enervate')
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with unfamiliar vocabulary that sounds like another word (e.g., 'enervate' vs 'energize').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify word meanings rather than relying on intuitive sound-alikes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-neutral language: avoid default 'he'; prefer phrasing that omits pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional use of 'he' is politically incorrect; alternatives like 'he/she' or 'they' can be awkward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best solution: rephrase sentences to avoid pronouns altogether where practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen vs en dash for naming collaborations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use en dash (–) rather than hyphen (-) to denote collaborations (e.g., 'Riemann–Lebesgue lemma') to avoid unintended connotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may change hyphens to en dashes; be aware of typographic conventions (en dash also denotes ranges like 'pages 324–386').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'if' vs 'whether'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If' and 'whether' have different meanings and contexts of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow examples like: 'Go to the window and see whether it is raining; if it is raining, then let Fido inside.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep 'infer' vs 'imply' distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Assumptions imply a conclusion; a reader infers a conclusion from assumptions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise verbs: assumptions imply, a person infers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'its' vs 'it's' correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It's' denotes 'it is' contraction; 'its' denotes possessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use an apostrophe for possessive pronouns (its, hers, his, theirs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay vs lie: transitive vs intransitive
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Lay' is transitive (acts on an object); 'lie' is intransitive. Past tense of 'lie' is 'lay'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of tense and transitivity to avoid errors (e.g., 'I shall lie down' vs 'Lay the book down').

rubrics_metrics.name: Less vs fewer: use by countability
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Fewer' compares discrete counts; 'less' compares quantity or continua.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., prefer 'Ten items or fewer' (discrete) and use context-specific judgments for mathematical comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the serial (Oxford) comma in lists
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting a comma-separated list, put a comma after every item except the last (the serial comma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'the good, the bad, and the ugly' rather than 'the good, the bad and the ugly' to avoid unintended links between items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick a standard for numbers and be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Different sources give different cutoffs for when to use words vs numerals; for mathematicians consistency matters more than cutoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a style for numbers (e.g., write out small numbers) and apply it consistently across the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Obviously', 'Clearly', 'Trivially'
rubrics_metrics.description: These words often bully the reader or conceal gaps in reasoning; many published errors have been prefaced with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove or justify their use; do not use them as smoke screens for unproven steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overused vague words ('very', 'most', 'nice', 'interesting')
rubrics_metrics.description: Overused modifiers add little meaning and can signal lack of substantive content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise descriptions; scrutinize every word for contribution to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural forms of foreign nouns: use correct singular/plural
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish singular vs plural forms of borrowed words (e.g., 'maximum' vs 'maxima', 'datum' vs 'data', 'criterion' vs 'criteria').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise when using foreign plurals to avoid common student errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive apostrophes: use '’s' for singular possessives; plural possessives drop terminal 's'
rubrics_metrics.description: Form singular possessives with '’s' (Pythagoras’s society); plural possessives use only an apostrophe (students' confusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle collective nouns specially (e.g., 'the people's choice'), and avoid extraneous apostrophes (e.g., TLAs not TLA's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance precision with custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes precision suggests a different term than custom; custom prevails for understandability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware when inventing terminology or notation that custom may override pedantic precision for reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-verb agreement: focus on the grammatical subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure subject and verb agree; identifying the root subject (omitting prepositional phrases) helps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'The set of all morphisms is compact.' Check by removing 'of ...' to see the root sentence 'The set is compact.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague demonstratives ('this', 'that', 'these', 'those') without clear referent
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Because of this, we decided that' leave 'this' or 'that' unclear; such vagueness can produce ambiguity often influenced by reader assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat nouns rather than rely on potentially vague pronouns; use explicit referents, especially across sentences or clauses.
